Braxton Bragg. A Confederate general during the American Civil War from eighteen seventeen to eighteen seventy-six, noted for tactical competence but crippled by poor judgment, excessive caution, and a volatile personality that alienated subordinates and superiors alike. His command of the Army of Tennessee saw mixed success in crucial battles across the western theater. He remains controversial among historians, sometimes praised for fighting well against odds, more often critiqued for squandering opportunities and failing to capitalize on victories.

A regular Army officer, Bragg graduated from West Point in eighteen thirty-seven and served with distinction in the Mexican-American War, earning a reputation as a skilled artillery commander. He transferred to Confederate service in eighteen sixty-one and commanded forces at Fort Sumter, then rose rapidly through the ranks despite limited political connections. His professionalism initially impressed President Jefferson Davis.

Bragg assumed command of the Army of Tennessee after Albert Sidney Johnston's death at Shiloh in April eighteen sixty-two. He led the army for two crucial years across the western theater. He won the Battle of Chickamauga in September eighteen sixty-three through superior numbers and tactical coordination, but failed to press his advantage or pursue the defeated Union army effectively. This hesitation cost him the opportunity to achieve a decisive victory.

Bragg repeatedly clashed with his generals, including James Longstreet and Leonidas Polk, over tactics and resources. His contentious nature eroded morale and cohesion in his command. After his removal from field command in eighteen sixty-four, he served as military advisor to President Davis. He died in poverty in eighteen seventy-six, largely forgotten despite his significant role in the war.
